title: Al-Fajr: the orphan, again
hookLine: no, you don't honor the orphan or urge feeding the poor, and you love wealth too much (89:17–20)

cards: Listen to how people talk when life goes well. I worked hard. I earned this.
Things are finally going my way. And when it goes badly: why me? What did I do to deserve this?
Both sound natural. Both are about me. Al-Fajr catches that exact habit, reading every good day as a reward and every hard day as an insult, and then it does something sharp.
It changes the subject to someone else entirely, someone this path has met twice already: the orphan.

teach.b: Verses fifteen and sixteen show a person tested two ways. Given honor and comfort, he says: my Lord has honored me. Given a tight, narrow provision: my Lord has humiliated me.
Then verse seventeen, in Pickthall's words: "Nay, but ye (for your part) honour not the orphan." The tables turn. You think the question is whether God honors you.
The surah asks whether you honor the one with no one. Then three more. You don't urge each other to feed the poor.
You swallow up inheritance, greedily; some commentators say this meant taking the shares of orphans and women, who couldn't defend them. And you love wealth with a love that has no bottom.
This is the orphan's third visit on this stretch of the path.
Ad-Duha: don't be harsh with the orphan. Al-Balad: feed an orphan who's a relative, on a day of hunger. Now here.

And Ad-Duha tied the orphan to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ himself, in Pickthall's words: Did He not find thee an orphan? The biographies say his father died before he was born, and his mother while he was still small.

teach.h: THE THIRD TIME ON THIS PATH.
teach.b: A hadith in Bukhari says he held up two fingers, side by side, and said that he and the one who cares for an orphan will be in Paradise like this. Notice the verb, too.
Honor, tukrimun, the same verb the man used about himself: my Lord has honored me. He wants honor; the surah asks him to give it. An orphan isn't a project.
The surah asks for dignity, and asks you to urge others toward it, not only to give quietly yourself.

how: Caring for orphans is a long-standing Muslim practice: many sponsor an orphan through a charity, support orphanages, or take in relatives' children, recalling that the Prophet was himself an orphan.

o: daybreak, the name of Surah eighty-nine
the reckoning that follows a person's death
the duty to honor and feed an orphan

games.q: what's inside the verses — tap the pairs.
p: you honor: the verb of "my Lord honored me"
the Prophet and the orphan's carer

s: the Prophet Muhammad grew up an orphan
Ad-Duha says so: did He not find thee an orphan (93:6)? the biographies add that he lost both parents young.
Al-Fajr only asks people to feed the poor themselves
it faults them for not urging one another to feed the poor, too.
the surah treats hard times as proof that God has humiliated someone
that's the human reaction it quotes and corrects.

games.q: a man says: my Lord has honored me, when life is good, and humiliated me, when it's hard. how does the surah answer?
o: it agrees: good times show God's favor
it turns to how he treats the orphan and the poor
it tells him to stop complaining
games.why: Nay: you don't honor the orphan (89:17). the question shifts from how God treats you to how you treat the one with no one.

practice: Think of a child who has lost a parent: one you know, a friend's child, a student, a neighbor, or one you'll never meet. Hold them in mind with respect, not pity.
Then settle on one thing you could do: a gift to a charity that cares for orphans, a message to a grieving family, time with a child who needs a steady adult.

wordCard.voice: Al-Fajr. The dawn, Surah eighty-nine, which asks not whether God honors you, but whether you honor the orphan. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the orphan, a child who has lost a father; the word also names a single, unmatched pearl.

carryVoice: Your line: honor the orphan. Not only help the one with no one: honor. Day one hundred ninety-seven, done.

sources.q: Nay, but ye (for your part) honour not the orphan
